title: Supreme Court Refuses to Restore Immigration Judges' Power to Shelve Deportation Cases
excerpt: A one-sentence emergency order leaves in place the Trump administration's same-day settlement with Texas that ended administrative closure, a docket tool used in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases.
body:
• The US Supreme Court on Tuesday refused to reinstate immigration judges' authority to temporarily shelve deportation cases, a practice known as administrative closure.
  • The one-sentence order, with no public dissent, leaves in place a same-day settlement between the Trump administration and Texas that a federal judge approved on June 22, permanently blocking the Biden-era rule nationwide.
  • Administrative closure has been used in hundreds of thousands of cases over decades, often while a person's visa petition or criminal appeal was pending elsewhere.
  • For anyone in immigration proceedings: cases can no longer be paused off the active docket by a judge on this ground, so pending cases move forward toward a decision.

The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice, Reuters reported. The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities, including Baltimore, and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt the deal ending the practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues.

The court's decision came as a brief, one-sentence order with no explanation, as is common for emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented.

What administrative closure did

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person were pending that could prevent removal — a visa petition working its way through USCIS, or an appeal of a criminal conviction. The practice has been applied in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases over the years. In 2024, the Biden administration adopted a regulation formally codifying it, concluding it let judges manage caseloads efficiently and promoted fair treatment. That regulation replaced a 2020 rule from Trump's first term that had been judicially blocked.

https://x.com/KimKatieUSA/status/2115135519902536073

Critics, including Texas and the Trump administration, have said administrative closure allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty. Texas argued in its lawsuit that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country." Ending the practice is part of Trump's hardline approach toward immigrants.

A lawsuit filed and settled on the same day

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Executive Office for Immigration Review — the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts — announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge. The administration and Texas then filed their agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day the state sued to challenge the procedure. US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls swiftly approved it the same day, declaring the Biden rule unlawful and blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider Centro Legal de la Raza sought to intervene to defend the rule, but O'Connor rejected their bid. The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending appeal, and the Supreme Court has now declined as well. The cities told the justices the administration had circumvented federal agency-procedure law by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked, writing that "the need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception," as Reuters' syndicated report detailed.

"Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country."

— Baltimore and co-litigants, represented by Democracy Forward

What changes for people in proceedings

The litigants and their lawyers from Democracy Forward said in a statement that "this dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny." Representatives of the Justice Department and the Texas attorney general's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The practical consequence is immediate. A person whose deportation case might previously have been shelved while, for example, a family visa petition or an employment-based green card process ran its course elsewhere must now keep litigating the removal case on the court's timetable. For Indian nationals in removal proceedings — including former H-1B workers whose status lapsed while a green card application sat in the decades-long backlog — administrative closure was one of the few tools that kept a case dormant without a deportation order. That tool is now gone unless the underlying litigation, which continues, ultimately restores it.
